summary.text: Define \(c_0=2,\ c_1=56\) and \(c_{n+2}=-4c_{n+1}-64c_n\). Eliminating the even-indexed terms from the fourth-order recurrence shows that \(b_n=a_{2n+1}\) satisfies \(b_{n+3}=-48b_{n+2}+3072b_{n+1}+262144b_n\); direct algebra shows \(c_n^2\) satisfies the same recurrence, and the first three values agree, so \(a_{2n+1}=c_n^2\) for all \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
c_0=2,\qquad c_1=56,
\]
and
\[
c_{n+2}=-4c_{n+1}-64c_n\qquad(n\ge 0).
\tag{2}
\]
We will prove the stronger identity
\[
a_{2n+1}=c_n^2
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(n\ge 0\).

First we derive a recurrence involving only odd-indexed terms of \(a\). We claim that, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
a_{2k+7}=-48a_{2k+5}+3072a_{2k+3}+262144a_{2k+1}.
\tag{4}
\]
To prove this, abbreviate
\[
x_j=a_{2k+j}\qquad(0\le j\le 7).
\]
Applying (1) four times, at the consecutive indices \(2k,2k+1,2k+2,2k+3\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_4&=-4x_3+256x_1+4096x_0,\\
x_5&=-4x_4+256x_2+4096x_1,\\
x_6&=-4x_5+256x_3+4096x_2,\\
x_7&=-4x_6+256x_4+4096x_3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]
Using the equation for \(x_6\) in the equation for \(x_7\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_7
&=-4(-4x_5+256x_3+4096x_2)+256x_4+4096x_3\\
&=16x_5+3072x_3-16384x_2+256x_4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]
The equation for \(x_5\), multiplied by \(64\), says
\[
64x_5=-256x_4+16384x_2+262144x_1.
\tag{7}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
-16384x_2+256x_4=-64x_5+262144x_1.
\tag{8}
\]
Substituting (8) into (6) yields
\[
x_7=-48x_5+3072x_3+262144x_1,
\]
which is exactly (4). Thus the odd-indexed subsequence of \(a\) satisfies a third-order linear recurrence.

We next show that the squares of the auxiliary sequence \(c\) satisfy the same recurrence. For every \(m\ge 0\), equation (2) gives
\[
c_{m+2}=-4c_{m+1}-64c_m.
\tag{9}
\]
Applying (2) once more and then using (9),
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{m+3}
&=-4c_{m+2}-64c_{m+1}\\
&=-4(-4c_{m+1}-64c_m)-64c_{m+1}\\
&=256c_m-48c_{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
We claim that
\[
c_{m+3}^2=-48c_{m+2}^2+3072c_{m+1}^2+262144c_m^2.
\tag{11}
\]
Indeed, put \(u=c_m\) and \(v=c_{m+1}\). Then (9) and (10) become
\[
c_{m+2}=-64u-4v,
\qquad
c_{m+3}=256u-48v.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&-48c_{m+2}^2+3072c_{m+1}^2+262144c_m^2\\
&\quad=-48(-64u-4v)^2+3072v^2+262144u^2\\
&\quad=-48(4096u^2+512uv+16v^2)+3072v^2+262144u^2\\
&\quad=65536u^2-24576uv+2304v^2\\
&\quad=(256u-48v)^2\\
&\quad=c_{m+3}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (11).

It remains to establish (3). We first check its first three cases.

For \(n=0\),
\[
a_{2\cdot 0+1}=a_1=4=2^2=c_0^2.
\]
For \(n=1\),
\[
a_{2\cdot 1+1}=a_3=3136=56^2=c_1^2.
\]
For \(n=2\), first use (1) to calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4(3136)+256(4)+4096(-1)\\
&=-15616,
\end{aligned}
\]
and then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
&=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
&=-4(-15616)+256(176)+4096(4)\\
&=123904.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand, (2) gives
\[
c_2=-4c_1-64c_0=-4(56)-64(2)=-352,
\]
and
\[
c_2^2=(-352)^2=123904.
\]
Hence \(a_5=c_2^2\), proving (3) for \(n=2\).

Now suppose, for some \(m\ge 0\), that (3) is already known at the three consecutive indices \(m,m+1,m+2\); that is,
\[
a_{2m+1}=c_m^2,
\qquad
a_{2m+3}=c_{m+1}^2,
\qquad
a_{2m+5}=c_{m+2}^2.
\tag{12}
\]
Using the odd-term recurrence (4), followed by (12) and then the square recurrence (11), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2m+7}
&=-48a_{2m+5}+3072a_{2m+3}+262144a_{2m+1}\\
&=-48c_{m+2}^2+3072c_{m+1}^2+262144c_m^2\\
&=c_{m+3}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(2m+7=2(m+3)+1\), this is precisely (3) at index \(m+3\). Starting from the three established cases \(n=0,1,2\), this three-step induction proves (3) for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

Finally, for each \(n\), the number \(c_n\) is an integer and (3) gives
\[
a_{2n+1}=c_n^2.
\]
Thus every odd-indexed term \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square, as claimed.
